In the mathematical field of [[Riemannian geometry]], the '''Berger spheres''' form a special class of examples of [[Riemannian manifold]]s diffeomorphic to the [[3-sphere]]. They are named for [[Marcel Berger]] who introduced them in 1962.

==Geometry of the Berger spheres==
The [[Lie group]] [[special unitary group|{{math|SU(2)}}]] is [[diffeomorphic]] to the [[3-sphere]]. Its [[Lie algebra]] is a three-dimensional real vector space spanned by
: <math>u_1 = \begin{pmatrix}
    0 & i \\
    i & 0
  \end{pmatrix}, \quad
  u_2 = \begin{pmatrix}
    0 & -1 \\
    1 &  0
  \end{pmatrix}, \quad
  u_3 = \begin{pmatrix}
    i &  0 \\
    0 & -i
  \end{pmatrix}~,
</math>
which are complex multiples of the [[Pauli matrices]]. It is direct to check that the [[commutator]]s are given by {{math|[''u''<sub>1</sub>, ''u''<sub>2</sub>] {{=}} 2''u''<sub>3</sub>}} and {{math|[''u''<sub>1</sub>, ''u''<sub>3</sub>] {{=}} −2''u''<sub>2</sub>}} and {{math|[''u''<sub>2</sub>, ''u''<sub>3</sub>] {{=}} 2''u''<sub>1</sub>}}. Any positive-definite [[inner product]] on the Lie algebra determines a left-invariant Riemannian metric on the Lie group. A '''Berger sphere''' is a metric so obtained by making the inner product on the Lie algebra have matrix
:<math>\begin{pmatrix}t&0&0\\ 0&1&0\\ 0&0&1\end{pmatrix}</math>
relative to the basis {{math|''u''<sub>1</sub>, ''u''<sub>2</sub>, ''u''<sub>3</sub>}}. Here {{mvar|t}} is a positive number to be freely chosen; each choice produces a different Berger sphere. If it were chosen negative, a [[Lorentzian metric]] would instead be produced. Using the [[Koszul formula]] it is direct to compute the [[Levi-Civita connection]]:
:<math>\begin{align}
\nabla_{u_1}u_2 &= (2-t)u_3&\nabla_{u_2}u_1&=-tu_3\\ \nabla_{u_2}u_3&=u_1& \nabla_{u_3}u_2&=-u_1\\ \nabla_{u_3}u_1&=tu_2&\nabla_{u_1}u_3&=(t-2)u_2.\end{align}</math>
The [[curvature|curvature operator]] has eigenvalues {{math|''t'', ''t'', 4 − 3''t''}}. The left-invariant Berger metric is also right-invariant if and only if {{math|''t'' {{=}} 1}}.{{sfnm|1a1=Petersen|1y=2016|1loc=Section 4.4.3}}

The left-invariant vector field on {{math|SU(2)}} corresponding to {{math|''u''<sub>1</sub>}} (or to any other particular element of the Lie algebra) is tangent to the circular fibers of a [[Hopf fibration]] {{math|SU(2) → S<sup>2</sup>}}.{{sfnm|1a1=Thurston|1y=1997|1loc=Section 2.7}} As such, the Berger metrics can also be constructed via the Hopf fibration, by scaling the tangent directions to the fibers. Unlike the above construction, which is based on a Lie group structure on the 3-sphere, this version of the construction can be extended to the more general Hopf fibrations {{math|''S''<sup>2''n'' + 1</sup> → '''CP'''<sup>''n''</sup>}} of odd-dimensional spheres over the [[complex projective space]]s, using the [[Fubini–Study metric]].

==Significance==
A well-known inequality of [[Wilhelm Klingenberg]] says that for any smooth Riemannian metric on a closed orientable manifold of even dimension, if the [[sectional curvature]] is positive then the [[injectivity radius]] is greater than or equal to {{math|{{frac|π|''K''<sup>1/2</sup>}}}}, where {{mvar|K}} is the maximum of the sectional curvature. The Berger spheres show that this does not hold if the assumption of even-dimensionality is removed.{{sfnm|1a1=Cheeger|1a2=Ebin|1y=2008|1loc=Chapter 5|2a1=Petersen|2y=2016|2loc=Section 6.5}}

Likewise, another estimate of Klingenberg says that for any smooth Riemannian metric on a closed simply-connected manifold, if the sectional curvatures are all in the interval {{math|{{closed-open|1,4}}}}, then the injectivity radius is greater than {{math|{{frac|π|2}}}}. The Berger spheres show that the assumption on sectional curvature cannot be removed.{{sfnm|1a1=Cheeger|1a2=Ebin|1y=2008|1loc=Chapter 5|2a1=Petersen|2y=2016|2loc=Section 6.5}}

Any compact Riemannian manifold can be scaled to produce a metric of small volume, diameter, and [[injectivity radius]] but large curvature. The Berger spheres illustrate the alternative phenomena of small volume and injectivity radius but without small diameter or large curvature. They show that the 3-sphere is a [[collapsing manifold]]: it admits a sequence of Riemannian metrics with uniformly bounded curvature but injectivity radius converging to zero. This sequence of Riemannian manifolds converges in the [[Gromov–Hausdorff metric]] to a ''two''-dimensional sphere of constant curvature 4.{{sfnm|1a1=Gromov|1y=1999|1loc=Section 3.11|2a1=Petersen|2y=2016|2p=399}}

==Generalizations==
===Berger–Cheeger perturbations===
The Hopf fibration {{math|S<sup>3</sup> → S<sup>2</sup>}} is a [[principal U(1)-bundle]]. Furthermore, relative to the standard Riemannian metric on {{math|S<sup>3</sup>}}, the unit-length vector field along the fibers of the bundle form a [[Killing vector field]]. This is to say that {{math|U(1)}} acts by isometries.{{sfnm|1a1=Thurston|1y=1997|1loc=Section 2.7}}

In greater generality, consider a Lie group {{mvar|G}} acting by isometries on a Riemannian manifold {{math|(''M'', ''g'')}}. In this generality (unlike for the specific case of the Hopf fibration), different orbits of the group action might have different dimensionality. For this reason, scaling the tangent directions to the group orbits by constant factors, as for the Berger spheres, would produce discontinuities in the metric. The ''Berger–Cheeger perturbations'' modify the scaling to address this, in the following way.{{sfnm|1a1=Petersen|1y=2016|1loc=Section 4.5.4}}

Given a right-invariant Riemannian metric {{mvar|h}} on {{mvar|G}}, the [[manifold|product manifold]] {{math|''G'' × ''M''}} can be given the Riemannian metric {{math|''th'' ⊕ ''g''}}. The left action of {{mvar|G}} on this product by {{math|''x''⋅(''y'', ''m'') {{=}} (''y'' ''x''<sup>−1</sup>, ''xm'')}} acts freely by isometries, and so there is a naturally induced Riemannian metric on the [[Quotient space (topology)|quotient space]], which is naturally diffeomorphic to {{mvar|M}}.{{sfnm|1a1=Petersen|1y=2016|1loc=Section 4.5.4}}

===Canonical variation of a Riemannian submersion===

The Hopf fibration {{math|S<sup>3</sup> → S<sup>2</sup>}} is a [[Riemannian submersion]] relative to the standard Riemannian metrics on {{math|S<sup>3</sup>}} and {{math|S<sup>2</sup>}}. For any Riemannian submersion {{math|''f'': ''M'' → ''B''}}, the ''canonical variation'' scales the vertical part of the metric by a constant factor. The Berger spheres are thus the total space of the canonical variation of the Hopf fibration. Some of the geometry of the Berger spheres generalizes to this setting. For instance, if a Riemannian submersion has totally geodesic fibers then the canonical variation also has totally geodesic fibers.{{sfnm|1a1=Besse|1y=1987|1loc=Section 9G}}
